findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer
findings.whyItBreaks: A compromise, replacement, or transient bad response from the remote endpoint is executed as shell during every image build, allowing arbitrary code to be baked into the resulting image. The URL has neither an immutable version nor an integrity check.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Every image rebuild downloads and executes whichever bytes the remote URL serves at that moment. A compromised, replaced, or otherwise changed installer gains arbitrary code execution during the build and can alter the produced image.

findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer
findings.whyItBreaks: Every image build fetches and executes whatever https://example.com/install.sh serves at that moment. A compromise or unexpected update of that endpoint changes build-time code without a source-controlled review, potentially producing a malicious image.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors in the exported loader
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported wrapper discards it and returns "". That is indistinguishable from a present key whose legitimate value is empty, forcing callers to treat failed loads as real data.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error
findings.whyItBreaks: When Load returns ErrMissing, this discards it and returns "", exactly the value returned for an existing key whose stored value is empty. As an exported API, callers have no way to distinguish absence from a real empty value.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key status in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: For an absent key, Load returns ErrMissing, but this helper discards it and returns "". Callers cannot distinguish lookup failure from a key explicitly stored with an empty value.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, Run returned only after every result was sent. It now returns immediately after scheduling goroutines. A normal producer wrapper that calls Run and then closes results can close the channel before a goroutine executes its send, causing a "send on closed channel" panic.

findings.title: Wait for all result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run could not return until every result had been sent. The new goroutines allow it to return while sends are pending, so a caller that closes results after Run returns can trigger a "send on closed channel" panic; callers that consume immediately after return can also observe incomplete results.

findings.title: Wait for all result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each job is now sent from an untracked goroutine, so Run can return before any result is delivered. A caller that closes results or advances to dependent work after Run returns can cause a send-on-closed-channel panic or observe incomplete results; the previous implementation returned only after every send completed.

findings.title: Require admin status before allowing record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: For a session with isAdmin=false and a tenantId matching the record, this now returns true, allowing a non-admin to delete any record in that tenant. It also permits an admin from a different tenant to delete the record. Both cases were denied by the previous predicate.

findings.title: Require admin and tenant match before permitting deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Using || returns true for a non-admin whose tenant matches the record, and for an admin from another tenant. Either session can now pass the deletion authorization check despite failing one of the prior required conditions.

findings.title: Require admin and tenant match before allowing deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing `&&` to `||` authorizes a non-admin user for any record in their tenant, and authorizes an admin for records in any tenant. The prior predicate required both conditions for deletion.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures before saving settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts malformed JSON and validation failures into a normal Settings value. updateFontSize therefore cannot distinguish corruption from valid defaults: it changes fontSize and calls save, overwriting the original data with theme="light" instead of preserving the prior failure behavior.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of saving fallback settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts malformed JSON and invalid settings into valid-looking defaults. updateFontSize then cannot distinguish failure from legitimate settings and calls save with a new record such as {"theme":"light","fontSize":22}; before this change parsing threw at src/settings.ts:9-11 and prevented that write. This silently replaces an invalid/corrupt stored value rather than surfacing the failure.

findings.title: Preserve invalid-settings failures instead of returning defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed JSON or invalid fields now become an ordinary default Settings value. updateFontSize then serializes and saves that fallback, whereas it previously propagated the error and made no save. For example, updating an invalid stored value overwrites it with {"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>}, losing any recoverable preference data and making failure indistinguishable from legitimate defaults.

findings.title: Load artifacts from the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When `branch` and `verified` resolve to different commits, `builtFrom` identifies the branch commit while `artifacts` belong to the verified commit. Consumers receive a report with a false commit-to-artifact association.

findings.title: Read artifacts from the requested branch
findings.whyItBreaks: For a requested branch whose commit differs from `verified`, `builtFrom` is set to the branch commit but `artifacts` are fetched from `verified`. The report therefore misattributes artifacts to the wrong build.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from "verified", the returned report claims it was built from the branch commit while its artifacts are fetched from the verified commit. Consumers cannot reliably associate the reported artifacts with builtFrom.

findings.title: Preserve the requested entry limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, this returns all reversed entries instead of at most limit. renderFeed passes 20 and then copies every returned entry, so an input of 21 entries produces a 21-entry result despite its fixed 20-entry page allocation.

findings.title: Apply limit before returning the sorted entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than `all.length`, this returns every entry rather than at most `limit`. `renderFeed` passes 20 at line 9, then copies every returned item, so an input with 21 entries produces a 21-entry feed instead of 20.

findings.title: Restore the positive limit cap
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, this returns every reversed entry instead of at most limit entries. renderFeed passes 20, preallocates 20 slots, then copies every returned item; with 21 inputs it returns 21 entries.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest rows
findings.whyItBreaks: With entries such as [{ path: "old", size: 1, stale: true }], the output declares `# entry-count: 1` but emits zero entry rows. Consumers relying on the serialized count to validate or read the manifest receive a contradictory manifest.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest rows
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, rows contains only live entries while headerLines still receives entries.length. For example, one live and one stale entry produces `# entry-count: 2` followed by one row, causing consumers that trust the declared count to read a malformed manifest.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest entries
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, its row is filtered out but the unchanged header still receives entries.length. The resulting # entry-count disagrees with the number of serialized rows, breaking consumers that use the header to validate or read the manifest.

findings.title: Restore the exported legacy ID formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing exported FormatLegacyID is a source-incompatible API change: any downstream consumer calling it will fail to compile when upgrading, and can no longer produce the established LEG########## identifier format.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was a public export of this module before the change, but the module now exports only Order and orderTotal. Existing TypeScript consumers importing shippingQuote from src/orders fail to compile; ESM consumers fail module loading because the named export no longer exists.

findings.title: Preserve the public shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was an exported function from src/orders.ts and is removed outright. Existing consumers importing it from that module will fail to compile or load after upgrading; quoteShipping is exported only from a new module path.

findings.title: Keep active viewers on the read-only route

findings.title: Preserve active viewers' read-only handling
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer with fewer than five attempts now fails isEligible and handle returns "rejected" before reaching its existing viewer-specific "read-only" branch.

findings.title: Keep eligible viewers on the read-only path

findings.title: Do not require payment to save a draft
findings.whyItBreaks: For a draft with payment="missing", canProceed now returns false. saveDraft uses this shared predicate at src/actions.ts:9, so a previously saveable unpaid draft now returns "blocked" instead of "saved". Payment legitimately governs submission, but not persisting a draft.

findings.title: Do not require payment to save a draft
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is shared by submitOrder and saveDraft. An order with state="draft" and payment="missing" previously reached saveDraft's "saved" result, but now returns "blocked" even though saving a draft should not require payment.

findings.title: Keep saving drafts independent of payment
findings.whyItBreaks: For an Order with state="draft" and payment="missing", the new predicate returns false, so saveDraft returns "blocked". The prior implementation saved that draft; payment should govern submission, not persisting an unfinished draft.

findings.title: Load files from the requested channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: When the requested channel and stable resolve to different commits, the returned Snapshot labels itself with the requested channel's commit but contains stable's files. Consumers therefore publish or inspect the wrong version.

findings.title: Read snapshot files from the selected channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, the returned Snapshot reports the channel's commit but contains the file list from stable. Consumers cannot reliably inspect or publish the files belonging to snapshot.commit.

findings.title: Read files from the requested channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The snapshot's commit and channel come from the requested channel, but files are read from "stable". When the requested channel and stable differ, callers receive a self-inconsistent snapshot: e.g. commit=mainHead with files from stableHead.

findings.title: Honor the new limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public `limit` parameter promises callers control over result count, but the implementation always uses `max_count = 10`. For example, `build("item", 3)` still returns ten values.

findings.title: Honor the limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: build('x', 3) still returns ten items because the implementation unconditionally sets max_count to 10. The new parameter therefore promises observable output capping that the function does not provide.

findings.title: Honor the limit parameter

findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int('-1') returns -1 because its body only calls int(). charge() relies on that name's promised invariant and returns -100, allowing a negative charge despite the public parser contract.

findings.title: Validate that parsed amounts are positive
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int("-5") returns -5 because its body only calls int(). charge() relies on that parser and produces -500, so a function now named as a positive-value validator permits negative charges.

findings.title: Enforce positivity promised by parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int('0') returns 0 and parse_positive_int('-1') returns -1. The new public name promises a positive result, while charge() consequently produces zero or negative cents instead of rejecting invalid amounts.

findings.title: Preserve the input DataFrame instead of mutating it
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation made df.copy() and updated only that copy. This version writes through df.loc, so callers that retain the source DataFrame observe their input changed after calling apply_values.

findings.title: Keep apply_values non-mutating
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation copies df before applying mappings; this version writes directly to the caller-owned DataFrame. Callers that retain df expecting apply_values to return a transformed copy will now observe their original data silently modified.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the reported base revision

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the declared base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: When `pinnedTag` resolves to a revision other than `latest`, `fromRevision` says consumers must replay from the pinned revision, but `changedPaths` describes changes relative to `latest`. Replaying this inconsistent changeset can omit or misapply paths changed between the pinned revision and latest.

findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when path does not exist (line 7). startup now immediately indexes that None at line 14, raising TypeError instead of retaining the prior default worker count of 1. Any startup using an omitted or not-yet-created settings file now fails.

findings.whyItBreaks: `load_settings` returns `None` when `path` does not exist, but `startup` now immediately subscripts that value. Previously this supported path returned the default worker count; it now raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable` and prevents startup.

findings.title: Restore a fallback when the settings file is absent
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None for a nonexistent path (app/config.py:6-7). The removed fallback previously supplied workers=1; startup now indexes None at line 14 and raises TypeError instead of starting with the documented-in-code default behavior.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, Charge logs the error then returns nil at line 19. Its exported error-returning API therefore conflates a declined/failed charge with a successful one, allowing callers to mark or act on an unpaid charge as paid.

findings.title: Return gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, Charge logs the failure then returns nil. Its exported API now makes a declined or failed charge indistinguishable from a successful payment, so callers may fulfill an unpaid order.

findings.title: Propagate failed gateway submissions
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge now logs it and returns nil. Callers therefore cannot distinguish a declined or failed charge from a completed one and may treat it as successful.

findings.title: Restore tenant ID to the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: The key is now derived only from name. Once tenant A reads a setting, tenant B reading the same name returns the cached value at lines 13-14 without calling its own store.fetch, leaking or misapplying tenant A's configuration.

findings.title: Keep the tenant ID in the cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A reads setting `theme`, its value is stored as `settings:theme`. A subsequent `settingsFor('tenant-b', 'theme', ...)` returns tenant A's cached value without calling `store.fetch`, causing cross-tenant configuration disclosure and incorrect behavior.

findings.title: Include the tenant in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: The first request for tenant A and name "theme" stores its value under "settings:theme". A later request for tenant B with the same name hits that entry at line 13 and returns tenant A's value without calling store.fetch, exposing incorrect cross-tenant settings.

findings.title: Serialize reservations across the persistence await
findings.whyItBreaks: The await splits the former atomic read-check-write sequence. With stock=1, two overlapping reserve calls can both read 1, both save 0, and both resolve true, allowing two successful reservations for one item. A concurrent load() can also be overwritten by the stale post-await stock.set().

findings.title: Serialize reservations before awaiting persistence
findings.whyItBreaks: Two concurrent calls with one unit remaining both read `remaining === 1` before either awaited save resumes. Both save 0, both return true, and the system accepts two reservations for one unit.

findings.title: Preserve the exported Inventory API or provide a migration
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing consumers can construct `new Inventory()` and synchronously use `reserve()` as a boolean. The new required Store constructor argument causes TypeScript callers to fail compilation, while unawaited JavaScript callers receive a truthy Promise even when inventory is unavailable.

findings.title: Serialize reservations across the persistence await
findings.whyItBreaks: With stock loaded as 1, two concurrent reserve calls both read remaining=1 before awaiting save. Both persist 0, both set local stock to 0, and both resolve true, so two reservations succeed for one unit.

findings.title: Keep zero-argument Inventory construction compatible
findings.whyItBreaks: Inventory is exported and previously had an implicit zero-argument constructor. Existing TypeScript consumers using new Inventory() now fail to compile; JavaScript consumers construct an instance with store undefined and a positive-stock reserve throws at the new save call.

findings.title: Preserve the synchronous reserve contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported reserve method changed from boolean to Promise<boolean>. Existing TypeScript consumers no longer typecheck, while JavaScript consumers using reserve in a conditional treat the Promise as truthy even when no stock remains.

findings.title: Stop multiplying millisecond backoff in retry
findings.whyItBreaks: `backoff(0)` now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but `retry` still multiplies it by 1,000 before sleeping. A first retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 minutes) rather than 1 second; capped retries wait over 8 hours.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds, but retry() still passes backoff(a) * 1000 to its millisecond-based sleep helper. The first retry is therefore delayed 2,000,000 ms (33 minutes) rather than 2,000 ms, and capped retries wait 30,000,000 ms (8.3 hours) rather than 30 seconds.

findings.title: Preserve retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: `backoff(0)` now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but `retry` still multiplies it by 1,000 before passing it to its millisecond-based `sleep`. The first retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (about 16.7 minutes) rather than one second; capped retries wait about 8.3 hours.

findings.title: Propagate the close error from Save
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is discarded. A close-time write failure is therefore returned as nil after a successful Flush, even though the previous implementation returned that error to Save callers.

findings.title: Return output close errors
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() discards its error. Previously, after a successful Flush, Save returned f.Close()'s error (base store/save.go:25); callers could detect delayed filesystem write or close failures. The new code returns nil instead.

findings.title: Propagate the output file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred Close result is discarded. Previously, a successful flush returned f.Close()'s error; now Save returns nil whenever Flush succeeds, even if the final file close reports a write/filesystem error. As exported API behavior, callers cannot distinguish a completed save from that failure.

findings.title: Include the end row in page windows
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns an exclusive end, but range(start, end - 1) also excludes end - 1, the last valid row. Every nonempty page loses one row; pages of size one render empty.

findings.title: Include the page endpoint in the window
findings.whyItBreaks: The half-open bounds calculate end as the exclusive endpoint, but range(start, end - 1) excludes end - 1. Consequently every page loses its final row; page_size=1 produces an empty page, and render_page/summarize silently omit rows.

findings.title: Include each page's final row
findings.whyItBreaks: The bounds helper defines end as exclusive, but range(start, end - 1) stops two positions before it. Thus a one-row page returns no rows, and every larger page silently drops its final row; render_page and summarize consequently omit records from their output.

findings.title: Return live cache entries before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: For a positive TTL, a newly stored entry has age less than ttlMs, so get deletes it and returns null. Once expired, the entry is returned instead. This inverts the cache's expiration behavior.

findings.title: Filter completed jobs without skipping adjacent entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during forEach shifts the next job into the removed index, but forEach advances past it. Given `[done A, done B, pending C]`, A is removed and B remains in the returned list.

findings.title: Restore live-entry behavior in TtlCache
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age 0, which is not greater than a positive ttlMs, so get() deletes it and returns null. Once an entry is expired, get() instead returns the stale value indefinitely.

findings.title: Do not splice while iterating completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an item shifts the next job into the current index, but forEach advances to the following index. For [{done:true}, {done:true}], the second completed job remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Return entries before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age 0, so it fails this condition, is deleted, and get() returns null. Once an entry is older than ttlMs, it is instead returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Remove every completed job
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during forEach shifts the next job into the index that has already been visited. For [done, done, pending], the second done job remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's jobs array
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation returned a filtered copy. This implementation splices the supplied array, so callers retaining jobs observe their queue unexpectedly lose completed entries.

findings.title: Restore the empty-input average result
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this returns NaN instead of the previous numeric result 0. Callers cannot use the returned value as an average without separately handling an undocumented NaN case.

findings.title: Avoid mutating the caller's rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort sorts in place. A caller that retains `rows` now has its original ordering overwritten after calling `busiest`, whereas the previous defensive copy preserved the input array.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average result
findings.whyItBreaks: For averageAmount([]), reduce produces 0 and division by rows.length produces 0 / 0, or NaN, instead of the previous 0 result. Callers can no longer safely use the returned value in numeric output or calculations.

findings.title: Do not reorder the caller's rows array
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows in place. Calling busiest(rows) now silently reorders the caller's array, unlike the prior defensive-copy implementation, so subsequent use of rows observes altered order.

findings.title: Preserve the zero result for empty input
findings.whyItBreaks: With rows=[], total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this returns NaN. The base implementation explicitly returned 0, so callers that display, serialize, or calculate with an empty aggregate now receive an invalid numeric value.

findings.title: Avoid mutating the caller's row array
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() reorders rows in place. Previously busiest() sorted a copied array, so callers could reuse their input order after querying the busiest row; this change silently changes that input order.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before deriving the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator orders numbers as strings. For scores 20, 100, and 3 with n=1, the reversed order is 3, 20, 100, so cutoff becomes 3 and topPlayers returns the first input player (20) instead of the 100-score player.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before reversing
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator sorts numbers as strings. For scores [100, 20, 9], this produces [100, 20, 9] before reversal and [9, 20, 100] afterward; with n=1, the cutoff becomes 9, so topPlayers returns the first input player scoring at least 9 rather than the player scoring 100. formatBoard consequently can display an incorrect first-place player.

findings.title: Sort numeric scores numerically before choosing the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: `Array#sort()` without a comparator compares string forms. Scores `[3, 20, 100]` become `[100, 20, 3]` then reverse to `[3, 20, 100]`; for `n = 1`, the cutoff becomes `3`, so `topPlayers` can return the first input player with score 3 instead of the 100-score player.

findings.title: Use a constant-time comparison for webhook signatures
findings.whyItBreaks: Plain string equality can reveal the length of a matching HMAC prefix through response timing. An attacker able to send repeated webhook requests can use that signal to recover a valid signature and reach processor(payload) without knowing the secret.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using `==` can exit at the first mismatched character, exposing signature-prefix timing differences to a remote attacker. The prior `hmac.compare_digest` avoided this leakage for the authentication decision in `handle`.

findings.title: Keep webhook signature comparison constant-time
findings.whyItBreaks: Ordinary string equality can return after the first differing character, exposing comparison timing correlated with the matching HMAC prefix. An attacker able to submit and time repeated webhook requests can use that signal to forge a signature and reach processor(payload).

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the transaction block exits before either balance update runs. If either subsequent UPDATE fails, the ledger permanently records a transfer that was not fully reflected in account balances; previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep balance updates in the ledger transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits immediately after `_record_ledger`. If either subsequent balance UPDATE fails, the ledger entry remains committed; if the second UPDATE fails, the source debit may also persist without the destination credit. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep all transfer mutations in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits immediately after `_record_ledger`. If either balance update then fails, the ledger permanently records a transfer while one or both account balances were not updated. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving a billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation explicitly used UTC fields. The new local-time getters return a different day on hosts west/east of UTC near midnight; for example, under America/Los_Angeles, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z now produces 2025-12-31 instead of 2026-01-01. sameBillingDay consequently can classify the same instants differently depending on the server timezone.

findings.title: Preserve UTC semantics for billing-day formatting
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation always derived the date in UTC. The new local-time getters produce a different billing day for the same instant on hosts in different timezones; for example, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z becomes 2025-12-31 on a UTC-08 host. This can assign charges or comparisons to the wrong billing day.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving the billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: This replaces deterministic UTC accessors with local-time accessors. For example, under America/Los_Angeles, billingDay(new Date("2026-01-01T00:30:00Z")) now returns "2025-12-31" instead of "2026-01-01". This also changes sameBillingDay's grouping behavior through its call to billingDay.

findings.title: Include tenant in the cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: A call for tenant A and account X stores A's Profile under X. A later call for tenant B and account X takes the cached branch at line 16 and returns tenant A's Profile without invoking fetchProfile, causing cross-tenant data disclosure and incorrect results.

findings.title: Include tenant in the memo key
findings.whyItBreaks: After fetching tenant A's profile for account X, a read for tenant B and account X hits the same `account`-only key and returns tenant A's Profile without calling `fetchProfile`. The exported Profile explicitly contains its tenant, so this returns incorrect cross-tenant data.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Two tenants with the same account value now share one process-wide memo entry. After tenant A caches account X, a read for tenant B/account X returns tenant A's Profile without calling fetchProfile, exposing cross-tenant profile data and producing the wrong tenant result.

findings.title: Propagate missing-key errors
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `Error("missing: <key>")`; it now returns `""`, which is a valid stored string value. Callers cannot distinguish a failed lookup from a real empty value. In particular, `loadAll` now returns partial-looking results containing empty strings instead of failing for an absent requested key.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw; it now returns "", which is indistinguishable from a legitimately stored empty string. Consequently, loadAll(["absent"], store) now returns [""] rather than failing, so consumers can process absent data as present.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors
findings.whyItBreaks: `load` is exported and now conflates a missing key with a key whose valid stored value is `""`. Consequently, `loadAll` returns an empty element for a missing key instead of propagating the prior `missing: <key>` error, so consumers can act on incomplete data without detecting it.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility for existing retry configuration
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing consumers using the exported Config shape `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` no longer type-check because both `retries` and `timeout` are required. Untyped/JS callers still passing `timeoutMs` get `config.timeout === undefined`; `Date.now() + undefined` is NaN, so the deadline guard never stops retries.

findings.title: Surface terminal retryBackground failures
findings.whyItBreaks: An exception from every attempt is discarded and the function returns `void`, exactly like a successful attempt or deadline expiry. As an exported API, this forces all callers to treat permanent failure as success.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config shape for retry
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing callers using the previously valid `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` shape no longer typecheck. Unchecked JavaScript callers instead read `config.timeout` as undefined, making the deadline NaN; the timeout predicate at line 10 is then always false, so retries continue past the requested timeout. `retries` is also newly required even though `retry` never reads it.

findings.title: Make retryBackground nonblocking or rename it
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported `retryBackground` API invokes `fn()` inline before returning. A caller using it to keep a request or UI path nonblocking instead waits for the callback and all immediate retries; this is the same foreground execution model already provided by `retry`.

findings.title: Report failure after retryBackground exhausts attempts
findings.whyItBreaks: An exception from every invocation is caught and discarded. Reaching the retry limit or deadline then returns void exactly like a successful invocation, so every caller of this exported API is forced to conflate failure with success.

findings.title: Expose terminal failure from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: When every invocation throws, this exported function catches every exception and returns `void`, exactly like a successful attempt. Callers cannot distinguish a completed background operation from one that exhausted all retries.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps.value` now publicly permits numbers, but number primitives have no `length`; for example, `value={123}` produces `len=undefined` (and TypeScript reports an invalid property access on the union).

findings.title: Handle numeric values without accessing `.length`
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps` now permits `value={42}`, but numbers have no `length`. TypeScript rejects this access, and if emitted JavaScript runs anyway the field renders `len=undefined` instead of a meaningful value.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now publicly accepts number values (line 2), but numbers have no length property. TypeScript rejects this access, and a JavaScript consumer receiving a numeric value would render "len=undefined" rather than a meaningful label.

score.error: critic produced no summary or checked list (likely malformed output)

findings.title: Retain the 64 MiB buffer for git output
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync now uses Node's default 1 MiB maxBuffer. The patch is collected through this helper at line 140, so a PR whose unified diff exceeds that limit terminates git with ENOBUFS; this occurs before the function's error handling and prevents any review or check from being posted.

findings.title: Preserve the 64 MiB git output buffer
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer restores spawnSync's 1 MiB default. The full PR patch is read through this helper at line 140, so a 1–64 MiB diff fails with ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER before a review can be posted.

findings.title: Keep a buffer large enough for review diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Without maxBuffer, spawnSync uses Node's 1 MiB stdout/stderr limit. runGithub uses this helper to capture the complete patch at line 140; a PR diff over that limit produces a max-buffer error/status failure, so line 38 throws and the review check fails instead of reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox for review runs
findings.whyItBreaks: This wrapper executes Codex in the repository supplied by opts.repoPath. Removing -s read-only means a configured workspace-write or danger-full-access default can let a review prompt modify or delete files in the repository being reviewed, defeating the wrapper's prior enforced read-only boundary.

findings.title: Restore the explicit read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Without the CLI override, codex exec loads its user configuration; a configured workspace-write sandbox can let an agent processing a review prompt modify opts.repoPath. The previous arguments enforced that this review wrapper could not alter the checkout.

findings.title: Restore the enforced read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: The wrapper previously forced every Codex review invocation into read-only mode. Without `-s read-only`, `codex exec` inherits the machine/user configuration, which may select `workspace-write` or `danger-full-access`; an untrusted review prompt or repository instruction can then modify the reviewed worktree or broader local files.

findings.title: Generate review input from the PR head's merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: The adapter still publishes the review against `headSha`, but now creates its patch and changed-file list from local `HEAD`. When `PR_HEAD_SHA` differs from the checkout (such as a PR merge checkout), the review analyzes a different revision and its inline comments may not apply to the submitted commit. Also, a current `PR_BASE_SHA` need not be an ancestor of the PR head; comparing it directly can include base-only changes as removals.

findings.title: Restore merge-base comparison against the supplied PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is a base branch commit that advanced after the PR branch diverged, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes base-only changes in reverse as though they were part of the PR. It also ignores PR_HEAD_SHA, despite the Bundle and GitHub review/check requests identifying that SHA as the reviewed commit. The review can therefore analyze and classify files from the checkout rather than the PR head, producing incorrect findings or omitted inline comments.

findings.title: Compute the review diff from the PR merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the current target-branch tip and that branch has advanced since the PR branched, `git diff baseSha HEAD` compares the two snapshots rather than the PR merge-base range. Base-only commits are therefore represented as removals and included in both `patch` and `changedFiles`, so the reviewer can analyze and attempt to comment on changes not made by the PR. These commands also disregard PR_HEAD_SHA when it differs from the checked-out HEAD, despite that SHA being used for the bundle and GitHub review commit.

findings.title: Preserve literal `$` sequences in prompt payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace treats `$&`, `$'`, `$`` and related sequences specially in a string replacement. A patch containing `const match = "$&"`, for example, causes `$&` at line 33 to become `{{PATCH}}` rather than remaining literal patch content; the same applies to bundle and findings JSON. Codex then receives a corrupted review or critic prompt.

findings.title: Preserve prompt payloads as literal replacement text
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets $&, $`, $', and $$ in a string replacement. A reviewed patch containing a common regex replacement such as "$&" is changed to "{{BUNDLE}}" when embedded at line 25 and to "{{PATCH}}" at line 33, so Codex receives corrupted source rather than the actual diff. The prior callback replacements inserted these payloads literally.

findings.title: Keep replacement values literal when building prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets $&, $`, $', and $$ in a string replacement. A reviewed patch containing, for example, "$&" is inserted into the critic prompt as "{{PATCH}}" rather than the literal source text; the same corruption applies to serialized bundle and candidate data. The model can therefore receive a malformed bundle/diff and produce an incorrect review.

findings.title: Keep the fallback review pinned to the reviewed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: When the primary POST fails and a newer commit is pushed before the fallback, omitting commit_id makes GitHub default the review to the PR's then-most-recent commit. The review body/event was produced for the captured headSha, so it can approve or request changes on code that was never reviewed.

findings.title: Keep the reviewed SHA on fallback submissions
findings.whyItBreaks: When the primary request fails (for example, because an inline comment is rejected), this fallback now omits commit_id. GitHub then defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit. If the PR advances while this review run is executing, Needlefish posts conclusions derived from headSha against the newer, unreviewed commit.

findings.title: Keep fallback reviews bound to the reviewed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the primary request fails (for example, due to an invalid inline comment) and the PR receives a newer commit before this fallback runs, omitting commit_id makes GitHub attach the review to the PR's most recent commit. The review result was computed for headSha, so a stale REQUEST_CHANGES review can block the new commit without being marked outdated.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating valid-looking ones
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously invalid required fields caused an explicit malformed-finding error. A finding that omits file and lineStart now becomes a P1 bug at file "" and line 0, so callers cannot distinguish invalid model output from a real finding and may publish or act on it.

findings.title: Preserve the exported strict-mode normalization contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the exported strict parameter is an incompatible TypeScript API change. Existing normalizeReview(raw, false) consumers no longer compile; JavaScript consumers silently have their argument ignored and no longer get the prior behavior of dropping malformed findings.

findings.title: Reject malformed finding fields instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Values that previously raised a malformed-output error now become valid-looking findings: an invalid severity becomes P1, an invalid category becomes bug, and missing required fields become empty strings or line 0. Callers can no longer distinguish invalid model output from a real P1 finding, so malformed reviews can be reported or acted on as genuine findings.

findings.title: Preserve the public strict-mode parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the exported strict parameter is a source-compatible break for TypeScript consumers calling normalizeReview(raw, false). JavaScript callers still run but no longer get the former tolerant behavior of dropping malformed findings; they receive the fabricated defaults introduced above.

findings.title: Reject malformed finding records
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid finding fields that previously raised an error are now converted into valid-looking P1/bug findings with empty paths, zero/invalid line numbers, and empty explanations. Callers of this exported normalizer cannot distinguish a malformed review response from a real finding.

findings.title: Preserve the non-strict review parsing mode
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported `normalizeReview(raw, false)` API is removed. TypeScript consumers passing the previously supported second argument no longer compile; at runtime, malformed findings that non-strict mode previously omitted are instead retained as fabricated defaulted findings.

findings.title: Keep the explicit repository when resolving manual PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before any checkout exists. Without -R "$REPO", gh pr view must infer a repository from the runner's working directory; it can fail in an uninitialized workspace or use a stale self-hosted-runner checkout. The failed substitutions are written as empty refs, allowing the later checkout to fall back to the default branch rather than reviewing the requested PR.

findings.title: Restore explicit repository selection for manual PR resolution
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so these commands run before actions/checkout. gh resolves a numeric PR against a local repository unless --repo or GH_REPO is supplied; this step supplies neither. On a fresh runner workspace it cannot identify the repository, and the command-substitution error is written as empty head/base outputs. Checkout then cannot target the requested PR.

findings.title: Restore an explicit repository for manual PR lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty and this step runs before actions/checkout. `gh pr view` therefore has no local Git remote from which to infer a repository, and neither command supplies `--repo` or `GH_REPO`. The ref-resolution step fails, so manually requested reviews never reach checkout or the review command.

findings.title: Reject malformed review output instead of returning an empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior required-field checks threw for malformed model output. Missing or wrongly typed summary/findings/checked/residual_risks now become "" or [], so callers of this exported API cannot distinguish a failed/malformed review from a legitimate review with no findings or residual risks.

findings.title: Reject malformed review envelopes
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizer previously threw for a non-object or any missing required review field. It now returns summary="" and empty findings, checked, and residual_risks arrays, making an invalid model response indistinguishable from a legitimate clean review. Callers therefore have no error signal with which to mark the review failed or needs-human.

findings.title: Reject malformed review output
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs such as null, {}, or a response missing findings/checked/residual_risks previously threw a malformed-review error. They now normalize to an empty summary and empty arrays, making a failed or truncated reviewer response indistinguishable from a valid review with no findings.

findings.title: Resolve the PR refs for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent. The checkout therefore uses github.ref rather than the input PR's head, BASE_REF defaults to main rather than the PR's base branch, and both PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA are empty. The review command still receives the requested PR number, but no longer receives the corresponding diff refs; the prior Resolve PR refs step explicitly queried those values for this path.

findings.title: Resolve the selected PR before manual review
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent. The checkout therefore falls back to github.ref (the workflow's selected ref, not the input PR), BASE_REF falls back to main, and both PR SHA variables are empty. Dispatching the documented pr_number workflow for a PR on another branch consequently runs the tool from the wrong revision and without that PR's resolved refs.

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent. The checkout therefore uses github.ref rather than the required pr_number's head, while PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA are passed as empty strings. Manual reviews consequently run the wrong checkout and receive no requested PR revision pair.

findings.title: Preserve buffer capacity for repository diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Without maxBuffer, spawnSync uses Node's 1 MiB output limit. runLocal passes the full output of `git diff <base> HEAD` through this helper, so a diff exceeding that limit fails with a buffer error instead of producing a review. The previous implementation supported diffs up to 64 MiB.

findings.title: Retain a buffer large enough for review diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer reduces git diff output capacity from 64 MiB to spawnSync's default 1 MiB. Reviewing any PR whose patch exceeds that size makes spawnSync fail with a max-buffer error; git() then throws, so runLocal aborts before it can submit the context bundle for review.

findings.title: Preserve the larger buffer for git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer changes spawnSync from the prior 64 MiB limit to Node's 1 MiB default. runLocal reads the entire merge-base diff at line 100, so ordinary large PRs now exceed the buffer and throw before reaching review.

findings.title: Keep review errors as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() throws, the check now concludes "neutral". GitHub treats neutral as successful for required status checks, so branch protection can allow a PR to merge even though Needlefish did not complete a review.

findings.title: Scope the PR diff to the configured repository
findings.whyItBreaks: Unlike the surrounding GitHub API calls, `gh pr diff` receives neither `--repo` nor the supplied cwd. In a multi-checkout or non-repository process directory, it can fail or resolve the same PR number in another repository, while the resulting review is posted to GITHUB_REPOSITORY.

findings.title: Keep review errors failing
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub treats a completed neutral check as successful for required status checks. If review() or posting the review fails, this now lets a PR satisfy a required Needlefish check despite the explicit "did NOT pass" error message; the action exit code does not protect repositories that require this custom check run. [GitHub docs](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/merge-and-close-pull-requests/troubleshooting-required-status-checks?apiVersion=2022-11-28)

findings.title: Keep review-error checks failing
findings.whyItBreaks: Any error from review or result posting reaches this catch block, but the emitted Needlefish check has conclusion "neutral". GitHub treats neutral as a successful required-check status, so a failed review can satisfy branch protection despite the error message saying it did not pass the PR.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer checkout on trusted main
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR head is now both the review target and the executable tool: a PR can change src/cli.ts (or package metadata/lockfile consumed by pnpm install) to skip findings, report a passing check, or use the write-scoped GH_TOKEN exposed to the review step. This defeats the review gate for every same-repository PR.

findings.whyItBreaks: After checking out the PR head, the workflow installs its dependencies and executes `src/cli.ts` from that checkout while supplying a token with `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write`. Any same-repository PR can therefore modify the CLI, package scripts, or dependencies to run arbitrary code on the self-hosted runner and forge or exfiltrate review credentials. findings.title: Restore a trusted reviewer checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow checks out the PR head at line 46, then executes its src/cli.ts here with GH_TOKEN. Same-repository PRs are permitted by line 24 and receive pull-requests:write and checks:write permissions, so a PR can modify the reviewer to create passing checks or otherwise act through that token, bypassing the review control.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from an available tool checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: This repository's HEAD tree contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has neither package.json nor src/cli.ts. pnpm install therefore has no project manifest, and even if it continued, the command at line 59 references nonexistent node_modules/.bin/tsx and src/cli.ts. Every review workflow run will fail.

findings.title: Preserve canonical severity normalization before defaulting
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped external JSON, but this now accepts only an exact uppercase severity. Inputs previously normalized successfully, such as " p0 " or "p1", now fail validation and are returned as P3, silently downgrading findings that should remain P0/P1.

findings.title: Preserve canonical severity normalization and fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: `normalizeReview` passes untyped review output into this exported normalizer. Inputs such as `" p1 "` or `"p1"` previously normalized to `"P1"`; they now become `"P3"`. Invalid or missing severities also changed from the established P1 fallback to P3, silently downgrading findings.

findings.title: Preserve canonicalization of severity strings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped external finding objects and passes them to normalizeFinding. A severity such as " p1 " or "p1", which the prior implementation canonicalized to P1, now fails the exact-membership check and is silently emitted as P3. This incorrectly lowers the reported severity of otherwise valid findings.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit sanitized env, spawnSync inherits process.env. Every run under GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, or GITHUB_API_TOKEN now exposes that credential to the Codex child process, where prompt-influenced commands can read and return it. The read-only sandbox does not redact environment variables.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an env option, spawnSync inherits process.env. This passes GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN into the Codex process, whereas the prior code explicitly removed them. A prompt-influenced Codex session can now access repository-scoped GitHub credentials.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env option, spawnSync inherits process.env. GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN are therefore available to the Codex process that receives prompt input; a prompt can cause those credentials to be read or included in Codex output, defeating the previous secret-isolation boundary.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before running the self-hosted job
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork PRs now reach the job, which checks out the fork SHA at line 23 and runs dependency installation and the checked-out CLI at lines 28 and 34 on a self-hosted runner. An attacker can add a package manifest with lifecycle scripts or alter the CLI in their fork, obtaining arbitrary code execution in the runner environment.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository gate before using the self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the job-level repository check allows pull requests from forks to run. The workflow checks out the fork's head SHA and executes its dependency installation and src/cli.ts on a self-hosted runner, letting an untrusted contributor execute arbitrary code in that runner's environment.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository gate before the self-hosted job
findings.whyItBreaks: A pull request from a fork now triggers this self-hosted job, checks out the fork's exact head SHA, and executes fork-controlled install and CLI code. A malicious fork can therefore execute arbitrary commands in the runner environment and access any runner-local credentials, workspace state, or network resources.

findings.title: Preserve zero-duration runner configuration
findings.whyItBreaks: A configured value of "0" previously produced a zero-delay timer; it now fails the changed guard and becomes the fallback. Consequently, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 waits 5000 ms before SIGKILL, and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 waits 2000 ms before resolving, breaking existing configurations that require no grace period.

findings.title: Continue accepting zero-duration runner settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior >= 0 check explicitly accepted 0. With this change, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 is silently replaced by 5000, delaying SIGKILL escalation by five seconds; NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 is similarly replaced by 2000, delaying timeout completion. This is a backward-incompatible change to two existing environment settings.

findings.title: Accept zero-duration runner settings
findings.whyItBreaks: A configured value of "0" was previously valid but now falls back silently. NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 therefore waits 5000ms before SIGKILL instead of scheduling it immediately after timeout; NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 similarly adds a 2000ms wait before resolving.

findings.title: Restore deep review for files outside six hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: The selected list is capped at six, and the removed tail-coverage pass was the only path that added changed files omitted by that cap or by mapping. The loop now deep-reviews only those six hotspots, while the final critic receives only a patch stat, so an omitted changed file can receive no diff-level review and the result can still pass.

findings.title: Propagate deep-review residual risks to the verdict
findings.whyItBreaks: Each successful deep review can return blocking residual risks, but this path now replaces all of them with an empty array before invoking the critic. A blocked/incomplete deep review is therefore indistinguishable from a clean one at verdict derivation, allowing a large review to report a non-blocking result despite unresolved material risk.

findings.title: Restore deep review for uncovered files
findings.whyItBreaks: Large bundles are limited to six mapped hotspots. Removing the tail hotspot means any changed file omitted by the mapper, or assigned to a seventh hotspot, is never included in a deep-review prompt. The critic receives only the resulting findings and patch stat, so a defect confined to that file can be returned as an apparently complete review.

findings.title: Keep failed deep reviews from aborting the whole result
findings.whyItBreaks: A malformed or failed deep-review invocation now rejects reviewLarge immediately. Previously the failure was recorded as a blocking residual risk and the remaining hotspots were still processed, allowing callers of the exported review() API to receive a ReviewResult rather than losing the entire large-PR review to one transient worker failure.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Successful deep passes can return residual_risks, including blocks:true when evidence is insufficient. This replacement always sends an empty array to the critic, so the critic cannot distinguish a clean review from one with a known blocking risk and can emit a non-blocking verdict.

findings.title: Deep-review every changed file
findings.whyItBreaks: Large bundles have more than 10 changed files, but selection retains at most six hotspots. Removing the uncovered-file tail means any files omitted by the mapper or truncated by this limit receive no deep review and no blocking residual risk, so a large PR can be reported without examining all changed code.

findings.title: Preserve deep-review residual risks
findings.whyItBreaks: A deep review can return residual_risks with blocks:true, but this path now ignores them and supplies residual_risks: [] to the critic. The downstream verdict therefore cannot distinguish a complete review from one that explicitly reported unresolved blocking evidence.

findings.title: Continue forwarding focus to large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: For bundles routed to reviewLarge, focus is no longer included in the map prompt and is no longer substituted into each deep prompt. A caller requesting, for example, a security-focused review of a patch over the large-patch threshold instead receives an unfocused review; the later critic cannot recover it because it receives only the candidate results and patch stat.

findings.title: Restore focus interpolation for deep-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews no longer inject `bundle.focus` into each deep-review prompt. A caller-supplied focus is therefore replaced by the unresolved/default prompt context, so large-PR review behavior differs from small reviews and ignores the requested review scope.

findings.title: Preserve deep mode in the map-pass bundle
findings.whyItBreaks: `bundle.deep` previously reached the map prompt but is now omitted, and no other remaining path reads it. Consequently, callers selecting deep mode produce the same map-pass input as callers that do not, silently disabling that control for large reviews.

findings.title: Propagate focus to large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: The large-review path previously forwarded bundle.focus to both map selection and each deep-review prompt. This change removes both propagation points, so a non-empty focus supplied by the caller reaches no runCodex invocation when isLarge() selects reviewLarge(), and the requested review area can be ignored.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For 59,500 ms, this computes minutes=0 and seconds=60, rendering "60s" instead of the rounded one-minute representation. At 119,500 ms it renders "1m 60s" rather than "2m 0s". The prior implementation rounded total seconds before splitting units, so both boundaries were normalized.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500ms, minutes is floored to 1 while the independently rounded remainder is 60, so rendered review stats show `1m 60s` rather than `2m 0s`. The same boundary issue renders 59500ms as `60s` rather than `1m 0s`.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500ms, `minutes` is 1 while the rounded remainder is 60, so rendered stats say `1m 60s` rather than `2m 0s`. The previous calculation rounded before deriving minutes and correctly carried this boundary.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger("0", label) now returns 0 even though its exported name and thrown-error contract promise a positive integer. Public callers can no longer rely on this parser to enforce a value greater than zero.

findings.title: Keep positive-integer validation
findings.whyItBreaks: `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` now returns `0`, despite the exported function name and retained error text promising a positive integer. Public callers can no longer rely on this validator to reject zero.

findings.title: Reject zero to honor the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` now returns `0`, although both its exported name and error contract promise a positive integer. Callers using it as validation can receive a non-positive value.
